title: Australian History · Episode 3
chapters: The 1967 referendum: what it really changed

units.t: Australian History. Episode three.
In this episode: Australia's Vietnam War, The 1967 referendum: what it really changed and Post-war Australia: migration and change.
Part one. Australia's Vietnam War.
It was Australia's longest war of the twentieth century and its most divisive.
Young men were chosen for it by a lottery of birthdays, and many came home to silence.
Why Australia went.
After the Second World War, Australian leaders feared communism in Asia, especially after China's communist victory in 1949 and the Korean War.
The domino theory held that if one country fell, its neighbours would follow until the threat reached Australia.
Vietnam was divided in 1954 into a communist North and non-communist South, and an insurgency grew in the South.
Australia also wanted to strengthen its alliance with the United States, formalised in the ANZUS treaty of 1951.
In 1962 it sent thirty military advisers.
In April 1965 Prime Minister Robert Menzies announced an infantry battalion, saying South Vietnam had requested help, a claim later questioned.
From 1966 the 1st Australian Task Force at Nui Dat focused on patient jungle patrolling.
The birthday ballot.
In 1964 the government introduced national service.
Twenty-year-old men had to register, and a lottery drew birth dates from a barrel.
If yours was drawn, you could be called up for two years.
From 1965 these conscripts, often called nashos, could be sent overseas, including to Vietnam.
Around 15,000 national servicemen served there, and some were killed.
The randomness troubled many Australians.
A young man's future, and perhaps his life, could depend on whether a marble bearing his birth date came out of a barrel.
Some refused to register or serve, and a few were jailed.
The ballot made the war deeply personal for families across the country.
Long Tan.
On 18 August 1966, D Company of the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, about 105 men, was patrolling near Nui Dat in a rubber plantation called Long Tan.
In a tropical downpour they met a far larger force of Viet Cong and North Vietnamese troops.
For several hours the Australians, with three New Zealand artillery observers, fought off repeated attacks, helped by intense artillery fire from the base and an ammunition drop by helicopter.
As darkness fell, armoured personnel carriers arrived and the attackers withdrew.
Eighteen Australians were killed.
Enemy losses were far higher, though exact numbers are disputed.
Long Tan became the best-known Australian action of the war, and 18 August is now Vietnam Veterans Day.
A divided country.
At first many Australians supported the war, but doubts grew as it dragged on, particularly after the Tet Offensive of 1968 showed the enemy was far from beaten.
Television brought images of the fighting into lounge rooms.
Groups such as Save Our Sons, formed by mothers of possible conscripts, campaigned against the ballot.
In May 1970 the Moratorium marches brought huge crowds into cities around Australia.
In Melbourne, led by Labor politician Jim Cairns, estimates ranged from 70,000 to 100,000.
Supporters of the war saw protesters as disloyal; many protesters saw the government sending young men to die for an unwinnable cause.
The divide split families, churches and friendships.
Withdrawal and coming home.
As the United States reduced its forces, Australia followed.
The task force left Phuoc Tuy in late 1971.
In December 1972 the Whitlam government ended conscription and freed men jailed for refusing to serve.
Almost 60,000 Australians served and around 520 died.
Vietnamese deaths ran into the millions.
Saigon fell in April 1975, and Australia later resettled tens of thousands of Vietnamese refugees.
Most veterans came home individually, often quietly, expected to slip back into ordinary life.
Some were abused by protesters, and some older veterans' groups were slow to welcome them.
Many struggled with post-traumatic stress, and concerns grew about Agent Orange, investigated by a Royal Commission in the 1980s.
In October 1987 tens of thousands marched in Sydney's Welcome Home parade, and a national memorial opened in Canberra in 1992.
The key idea: Fear of communism spreading through Asia, and the wish to keep the United States close, drew Australia into Vietnam.
Part two. The 1967 referendum: what it really changed.
More than 90 per cent of Australians voted Yes in 1967, the biggest win in referendum history.
Yet many people still believe it did things it never did.
The biggest Yes ever.
On 27 May 1967, about 91 per cent of Australians voted Yes to a question about Aboriginal people, and every state agreed.
It is the biggest Yes in referendum history, in a country where change is hard.
A proposal needs a majority of voters nationally and majorities in at least four of six states, and only a handful of more than 40 proposals have passed.
The result came from a decade of campaigning.
The Federal Council for the Advancement of Aborigines and Torres Strait Islanders gathered petitions, with leaders including Faith Bandler and Joe McGinness.
The 1965 Freedom Ride, led by Charles Perkins and students, exposed segregation in country New South Wales.
By the vote, the major parties backed Yes and there was almost no organised No case.
Two changes only.
The 1901 Constitution mentioned Aboriginal people only twice, and both times to exclude them.
Section 51 lists the subjects the federal Parliament can make laws about.
It gave power over 'the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State', which left laws about Aboriginal people to the states.
Section 127 said that in reckoning the numbers of the people of the Commonwealth, 'aboriginal natives shall not be counted'.
The 1967 referendum removed the words 'other than the aboriginal race in any State' from section 51, and deleted section 127 altogether.
That was the entire legal effect of the vote.
Myth: the right to vote.
One of the most common beliefs about 1967 is that it gave Aboriginal people the right to vote.
It did not.
Voting rights are set mainly by ordinary laws passed by parliaments, not by the Constitution.
Some Aboriginal people could vote in a few colonies from the 1850s and 1890s, although many were later excluded.
In 1962 the Commonwealth Electoral Act was amended to give all Aboriginal people the right to vote in federal elections.
The states moved at different speeds, and Queensland was the last to grant state voting rights, in 1965.
So by the referendum, Aboriginal Australians had the right to vote in federal and state elections, even though many still faced real barriers in practice.
Myths: citizenship and fauna.
Another myth is that the referendum made Aboriginal people citizens.
Australian citizenship was created in 1949, and Aboriginal people born in Australia were covered by it.
In practice, many were still denied rights by state laws controlling where they lived, worked and married.
A third myth says Aboriginal people were managed under a 'Flora and Fauna Act' until 1967.
Historians and fact checkers have found no such law, at federal or state level.
The myth probably spread because it captured how dehumanising the real treatment felt, but it is not accurate.
Correcting these myths does not shrink the referendum's importance.
It shows that its power was partly symbolic, and partly about which government held responsibility.
What it did change.
Removing the exclusion from section 51 meant the Commonwealth, not just the states, could now make laws specifically for Aboriginal people.
The federal government went on to create new agencies and programs, and in 1976 Parliament passed the Aboriginal Land Rights, Northern Territory, Act.
Deleting section 127 meant Aboriginal people would be included in official population counts.
Yet the change was neutral on its face.
The race power covers people of any race, and courts have since debated whether laws made under it must benefit the group.
Many campaigners felt real progress came more slowly than the 1967 hope promised.
Even so, the vote remains a landmark, and its date now marks the start of National Reconciliation Week.
The key idea: The 1967 referendum won about 91 per cent of the vote after a decade of campaigning by Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Australians.
Part three. Post-war Australia: migration and change.
'Populate or perish.'
After 1945, millions of migrants, the end of White Australia and new recognition of First Nations rights reshaped the country.
Populate or perish.
The Japanese bombing of Darwin in 1942 convinced Australian leaders that a small population was a danger.
They wanted more people for defence and industry.
Immigration Minister Arthur Calwell's slogan was 'populate or perish', and a Department of Immigration was created in 1945.
Australia first accepted about 170,000 displaced people from war-torn Europe.
Large numbers of British, Italian, Greek, Dutch, German and Maltese migrants followed.
Many British arrivals paid just ten pounds for the voyage, earning the nickname 'Ten Pound Poms'.
Between 1945 and the mid-1970s, roughly three million migrants arrived, many of them to work on nation-building projects.
The Snowy Mountains Scheme.
The biggest of those projects was the Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Scheme.
Built between 1949 and 1974, it has 16 major dams, seven power stations and about 145 kilometres of tunnels.
It diverts water from the Snowy River westward through the mountains, generating electricity and supplying irrigation water to the Murray and Murrumbidgee river systems.
More than 100,000 people from over 30 countries worked on it, many of them recent migrants who had been on opposite sides in the war.
More than 100 workers died during construction.
It became a symbol of post-war ambition and an emerging multicultural society, and it is still a major source of renewable electricity.
Ending White Australia.
Since 1901, the White Australia policy had restricted non-European immigration.
Officials could set a 50-word dictation test in any European language, designed to be failed.
The policy eased gradually.
The Colombo Plan brought thousands of Asian students to Australian universities, the test was abolished in 1958, and the Holt government loosened restrictions in 1966.
In 1973, the Whitlam government removed race as a factor in immigration selection.
The Fraser government accepted tens of thousands of Vietnamese refugees in the late 1970s and 80s.
Multiculturalism became official policy and SBS television began in 1980.
Today about 30 per cent of Australians were born overseas, roughly half have a parent who was, and over 300 languages are spoken at home.
1967 and land rights.
The 1967 referendum removed two discriminatory references from the Constitution: one excluded Aboriginal people from population counts, and the other stopped the Commonwealth making laws for them.
About 90.
8 per cent voted yes, the highest result of any referendum.
It did not give Aboriginal people citizenship or the vote, which they already had in law federally from 1962.
Instead it was a symbol of support that later underpinned land rights and heritage laws.
Activism grew.
Gurindji stockmen led by Vincent Lingiari walked off Wave Hill in 1966, first over pay and then over land, and in 1975 Gough Whitlam poured soil into Lingiari's hand.
The Tent Embassy rose in Canberra in 1972.
In 1992, months after Eddie Mabo's death, the High Court's Mabo decision rejected terra nullius and recognised native title.
Reckoning and reform.
The 1997 Bringing Them Home report documented the Stolen Generations, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children forcibly removed from their families by governments and churches.
It estimated that between one in three and one in ten children were taken between 1910 and 1970.
About 250,000 people walked across Sydney Harbour Bridge for reconciliation in 2000, and Kevin Rudd delivered a formal National Apology in February 2008.
The 2017 Uluru Statement from the Heart called for a First Nations Voice.
A 2023 referendum on a Voice to Parliament was defeated, with about 60 per cent voting no, and debate about treaties and truth-telling continues.
Wider change came too: equal pay decisions in 1969 and 1972, the Sydney Opera House in 1973, no-fault divorce in 1975, and Medicare in 1984.
The key idea: After the 1942 bombing of Darwin, Australia launched a mass immigration programme that brought about three million people by the mid-1970s.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What was the domino theory?
Answer. Falling countries would drag down neighbours.
Question two. What made the 1967 result so unusual?
Answer. An overwhelming Yes vote, carried in every state.
Question three. Why did Australian leaders push for a much bigger population after World War II?
Answer. Fear of invasion, as shown by Darwin, made defence a priority.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
